presentingComplaint: Generalised weakness, palpitations, and reduced urine output for 2 days.
history: 68-year-old man with known CKD stage 4 (baseline creatinine ~2.8 mg/dL, not yet on dialysis) and type 2 diabetes presents with a 2-day history of progressive generalised weakness, mild breathlessness, and palpitations. He reports his urine output has fallen sharply over the last 48 hours and he has had no bowel motions for 3 days. He was started on an ACE inhibitor and a potassium-sparing diuretic combination two weeks ago for poorly controlled hypertension, and has also been taking over-the-counter NSAIDs for knee pain over the past week. No chest pain, no fevers, no diarrhoea or vomiting. No history of missed dialysis (not yet on dialysis). No recent trauma or muscle injury.
examination: Alert but appears fatigued and mildly drowsy. No focal neurological deficit. Reduced muscle power globally (4/5) with diminished deep tendon reflexes. Irregular pulse noted on palpation. Mild bibasal crepitations. No peripheral oedema. Abdomen soft, non-tender. No signs of volume overload beyond mild bibasal crackles; mucous membranes dry suggesting reduced intake.

labs.ecg: Peaked T waves, widened QRS, loss of P waves, sine-wave pattern

imaging: Renal ultrasound: bilateral small echogenic kidneys consistent with chronic kidney disease, no hydronephrosis
differentialDiagnoses: Medication-induced hyperkalaemia (ACE inhibitor + potassium-sparing diuretic + NSAID)
Bradyarrhythmia from primary cardiac conduction disease
finalDiagnosis: Severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes secondary to acute-on-chronic kidney injury (drug-induced: ACE inhibitor, potassium-sparing diuretic, NSAID)
citations: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for Acute Kidney Injury 2012
AHA/ACC 2023 — Management of Hyperkalemia consensus recommendations
contraindications: Avoid further ACE inhibitor, ARB, potassium-sparing diuretic, or NSAID administration until potassium normalises and renal function stabilises
Avoid succinylcholine if intubation required (risk of exacerbating hyperkalaemia)
Use calcium gluconate cautiously in patients on digoxin (risk of digoxin toxicity precipitating arrhythmia)
edgeCases: Sine-wave ECG pattern and bradycardia represent a peri-arrest emergency requiring immediate IV calcium gluconate before other measures
Concurrent metabolic acidosis (bicarbonate 14) both contributes to and is worsened by hyperkalaemia; correction of acidosis is adjunctive, not primary therapy
Diabetic patients may have coexisting hyporeninaemic hypoaldosteronism (type 4 RTA) amplifying drug-induced hyperkalaemia
Distinguish from pseudohyperkalaemia due to haemolysed sample — repeat sample on a non-haemolysed draw only if clinically stable, not if ECG changes present
If refractory to medical therapy or with oliguric AKI, emergent dialysis is indicated
expectedMaiK: Flag this as a hyperkalaemic emergency: peaked T waves progressing to sine-wave pattern with bradycardia mandate immediate IV calcium gluconate for cardiac membrane stabilisation, followed by insulin-dextrose and potassium-removal measures (potassium binders/dialysis); stop all potassium-raising drugs (ACEi, potassium-sparing diuretic, NSAID) and evaluate for urgent dialysis given oliguric AKI on CKD.
